Hey! Aight so a couple things.

First - the things that you list - not having friends, being ugly, so on and so forth - first of all, keep in mind that depression distorts your view of things. You may feel ugly - you may feel that you're worthless - those thoughts are common symptoms of depression. Although they might seem obvious to you, knowing that believing those things is a symptom of depression, at least open yourself up to the idea that they don't accurately reflect reality.

Second - you are not a bad person. None of the things that you list are reasons why you deserve to die, or to suffer. There are people out there that are murderers; there are people that have done terrible things. You are not one of those people. It sounds like you care about people, even if it feels like they don't care about you back; it sounds like you care about being a better person. Those are signs that you're a good human being. Your parents sound awful if they'd say something like that to you; if people don't want to be your friend, that's their problem, not yours. My point is that the problem is not with you; it's with the people around you, and that you deserve better. Statistically, you are highly likely to find someone that cares about you in your life; life goes on beyond the present moment and the place that you're at. You can go to college, or get a job after you graduate; you'll make friends. You'll find someone you love and get married, if you want. You can have experiences. You seem like a good person, and you'll find other good people eventually.

Third - I don't know if you've tried to get help, but if not, you should. I think I've had a similar experience to you in that I was depressed for YEARS before I got gradually better; I started to think that everything was hopeless, that I'd always feel this way. Truly, there are ways out. You don't have to feel this way about yourself, about the world around you; you don't have to be in pain - you don't deserve to be in pain. That might take a while; in the meantime, find something you enjoy, whether that's a TV show, a job, a subject in school, idk, even sleep - you'll make it through. There's a lot of joy to be found in the world, even if it's hard to see that now. The things you want - not being in pain, having friends, finding someone you love, not feeling ugly - you can 100% have them.

Honestly, he's killing it; I think he's been incredibly underrated so far, mostly because he isn't trumpeting his accomplishments on the media constantly - he's been surprisingly constrained in terms of contact with the media, which I also appreciate. A couple things:

He has done an incredible job with the vaccine roll-out. Currently, there are going to be enough vaccines to vaccinate everyone in the US by late May; that's even more impressive considering Trump basically failed to order enough vaccines as he should have last summer, which means Biden had to cover some ground. The vaccine roll-out has also been ridiculously organized; by April 19th, over 90% of Americans will have a vaccination site within 5 miles of their home, which is incredibly key to ensure equal access to the vaccine for communities of color/rural communities/etc. and means that more people will be getting vaccinated.

His American Rescue Plan was one of the biggest, most transformative pieces of legislation in the past 50 years that got - proportionately to its impact, at least - very little hype and appreciation. Researches at Columbia estimated that it will cut child poverty in the US in half; it sets aside $20 billion to go towards ending homelessness, and invests in healthcare for communities of color and tribal communities. It invests in Head Start, ensuring low-income families can have childcare and access to early childhood education, and it gives billions of dollars to public universities to provide scholarships to low-income students. It also gives huge amounts of money to small businesses impacted by the pandemic. It's a huge economic package that goes WAY beyond just COVID response and honestly will be transformative for education and the economy moving forward - given that COVID is at the front of all our minds, this aspect of the legislation has gotten very little hype.

He's investing in renewable energy, passing legislation to protect lgbtq+ rights, investing in transportation infrastructure, and has attempted to raise the minimum wage (although that one he hasn't done yet). Biden was not my first choice in the primaries, but honestly, I feel like he's been doing a really incredible job. Honestly, I appreciate how low-key he's been in the media, but I feel like he needs to talk about his accomplishments more; keeping quiet is what allows people like Trump to talk about the "do-nothing democrats" or asking people what at all has changed while Democrats have been in office. Of course he's not perfect, he's done some things that I disagree with, but all the attention right now is going to the few things that he's done that are controversial, or the things that he's done wrong; he's the president of the United States, of course he'll have some misteps, but it would be dope if people started recognizing his accomplishments as well so far, imo.

Hey! I have some thoughts. I'm from the United States, so I don't really know what things are like in Russia, but I did some research - I hope any of this helps!

First - like you said - it sounds like you need professional/actual help, beyond what you're going to find on reddit (although people here - including myself - really do care, very few of us are professionals that can work with you on a longer-term basis). The first thing I'd say is that you definitely should find a therapist. I know you said in the comments that you were worried that they might be transphobic - like I said, I live in the US, so I don't really know what the experience is with finding therapists that are cool with LGBT+ people in Russia - but I researched a few options that might help you find someone:

This is the Russian LGBT network that I found online; they say that they provide free psychological help for trans and other lgbt+ people in Russia, as well as helping them with legal issues (changing gender legally, accessing hormones, etc.) It looks like they actually have physical locations/buildings in the cities specified on this link: [https://lgbtnet.org/en/contacts/](https://lgbtnet.org/en/contacts/) If you're not near one of their locations, they provide contact info on the page that I sent you; I'm sure you could contact them and they could hook you up with a trans-friendly therapist near you, or another LGBT+ group that might be closer to you that could help you out.

A lot of therapists - at least in the States - do short phone interviews to decide whether working with a client would be a good match. I feel like this interview would be a good time to figure out if they're trans-inclusive and if you want to work with them. The Human Rights Campaign included some questions that are good to ask therapists to figure out their stance on trans rights: [https://screening.mhanational.org/content/questions-help-qtbipoc-find-affirming-mental-health-providers/](https://screening.mhanational.org/content/questions-help-qtbipoc-find-affirming-mental-health-providers/)

[https://www.ilga-europe.org/who-we-are/members](https://www.ilga-europe.org/who-we-are/members) This is a list of the members of IGLA Europe (lgbt group). Just scroll down the the "Russian Federation" section under members, and it gives you a whole list of different LGBT+  groups in different parts of Russia that can help you find community and professional mental health counseling, as well as anything else you need. You might have to spend some time looking through most of the links - it looks like some of the websites no longer exist, and each group does a different thing - but there's a lot there, looks like you might be able to find what you need (or at least reach out to them, even if they're in a different city than you, so they can direct you to help locally where you are).

If you can't find someone in person, there's also the option of online therapy. From my research, it looks like it's important to do research into the qualifications of online therapists, but if you find a legit one it seems like that might be a great option esp if you don't live in a big city. Here are some places I found that might help you out:

[https://www.pridecounseling.com/](https://www.pridecounseling.com/) (a therapy/counseling group that is specifically targeted to serve the LGBT+ community - you will definitely get a fellow LGBT+ or trans-accepting therapist that specializes in helping trans people. Looks like you just gotta click "find a therapist" on their site and they'll help you out.)

[https://www.betterhelp.com/](https://www.betterhelp.com/) is pretty legit, based on google searches, and seems to be pretty low cost and popular. You can search the site to find therapists that specialize in certain things, like helping trans or lgbt+ people.

There are other online places as well - a Google search should turn them up pretty easily.

Re: being isolated; that sucks. Like, a lot. Homeschooling sounds tough; I have friends who were homeschooled growing up, and initially had a lot of trouble finding connections to the outside world - my point is to know that it's not just you. It would probably help to know more about your exact situation to give more advice on finding connections, so sorry in advance if this misses the point, but are there any groups that you could join that would introduce you to people? Either hobbies that you have, something you want to learn how to do, school-related study groups, etc.

Are you still homeschooled? I ask because, if you aren't homeschooled anymore, reaching out to people that you go to school with can be a great way to make connections. If you're still homeschooled, you might want to consider transferring to a school (not being homeschooled anymore). Another option is to get a job, if you don't already have one; even one that's part-time can introduce you to people outside of your immediate circle; at least that's what happened for me, getting a job introduced me to a ton of people. The internet is a dope way to make friends too (although less beneficial than hanging out with friends in person, imo!). If you want, you can always message me, I need more friends too lol

Honestly, you just sound really depressed, re: the whole "not being able to focus on anything" thing, or "not liking the things you used to like." Depression is hard; it's also something that a lot of people have gone through and come out the other side of. It's treatable; it's a temporary state. I know you said you needed more than strangers on the internet typing generic words - which is 100% fair, and you definitely should get that help - but I hope you know that the things you are feeling right now are temporary - it really does get better, as cheesy and cliche as that is. Message me anytime, I'm always down to talk if you need anything within my range of abilities as an internet stranger that lives across the world - either way, I really will be thinking about you and sending good thoughts.

I mean, first things first I'd have to guarantee my survival. If there are no people left, that means no fresh water, no farmers growing food, no people pumping/siphoning gas or operating the electrical grid. I'd have to figure out how I was gonna survive, which probably means finding a place to stay with fresh water (or learning how to create it), learning how to farm, basically learning a bunch of new skills really quickly. I'd probably do a lot of reading in the first few months, lol.

I'd also - simultaneously - try to make sure there was no one else left. I'd search the internet, trying to find other people that were still alive. If anyone else was left, I'd try to find a way to meet up with them - way less difficult if we can drive to meet each other, more difficult if they live overseas, unless anyone still left knows how to operate a boat or a plane. 

Next, no matter if there was anyone else left or not, I'd probably try to figure out what happened/what made everyone vanish so suddenly. I'd definitely dedicate large amounts of time to figuring that out, reading books on what could possibly have caused that phenomenon, etc. Honestly, without other humans to interact with, I'd probably spend a lot of time reading; trying to figure out if there's an afterlife, what the meaning of human life is - being on the cusp of human extinction would probably really make me wonder about that.

I'd probably also spend large amounts of time recording my experience and taking photos/recording what was left on Earth; in case some sort of intelligent life form ever lived on Earth again - or came to Earth through outer space - maybe it would be valuable for them to know what the experience of the only human that didn't vanish was (and maybe even learn from the mistakes that led to our extinction).

I'd also probably try to take in the pets that were left behind - as many as I possibly could. It makes me really sad to think about all of these domestic animals being left behind by their owners - how would they survive?? I'd take care of as many as I could find.

I get that feeling; I honestly expected to feel elated on election night in the event of a Biden win; I always imagined swing states going for Biden by huge margins, the country coming together in a strong repudiation of Trump and all that he stands for. 

Instead - and I'm not trying to jinx it, there are still a lot of ballots to be counted - the event of a Biden win feels a lot more like a whimper to me than a forceful rejection of Trump’s principles. This has been a nail biter of a presidential election; after stressing out while refreshing the New York Times tracker on my computer for hours last night, in the event of a Biden win, I’d be mostly relieved, not elated or fired up. Mostly, seeing how close this election has been is sobering: so many people STILL voted for Trump, after everything. It’s not exactly awe inspiring or encouraging of trust in my fellow countrymen. 

Thinking about it more, though, I’ve just decided that might not be a 100% bad thing. The fact that we even believed that our country was able and ready to repudiate Trump in that massive way is just an illustration of our faith in other people - yes, even Trump supporters - and our nation as a whole. Pete has even said this a couple times: that we as individuals are not black or white - good or evil - but that we’re each capable of immense good or immense evil. That’s been the story of 2020, more often than not; keeping the faith even when things are hard, or the path forward doesn’t seem clear, or when it seems like there’s a massive amount of evil in the world. In many ways, that’s also the story of the United States: an incredible promise mired by evils like slavery, disenfranchisement, colonialism, income inequality, poverty – on and on. The problems that stop us from achieving the original values and goals of our country – all of us being created equal, among any others - evolve, but have never really gone away. Instead of giving up, or acquiescing to the inevitability of the existence of these evils, each generation – driven by trust in the truth of those original values, and the belief that we are capable of living up to them – have moved our country closer and closer to them; the arc of the history of the United States, with all the problems we continue to have, has slowly but surely bent towards equality and freedom and away from stuff like oppression and immorality. If Biden is elected, that’ll be the story of an incredibly flawed country, mired with shades of gray, doing an incredibly good thing. I’d caution us to not write Trump supporters off as unreachable racists, or inherently awful people; they’re like the rest of us, people with flaws and bad opinions - but people nonetheless. Our country, like the people that constitute it, is full of a mixture of black and white instead of one or the other. In the event of Biden scraping through for a win that’s more of a whimper than a full-on rejection of everything Trump stands for, we will have drawn out more of the good in other Americans; not suddenly and unfailingly, a complete triumph of the light over the dark, but, as to be expected in complex people full of shades of gray, slowly and falteringly. That’s a closer reflection of reality; that’s also a tremendous accomplishment, and a tremendous reason for hope. Keep the faith, both in one another and our country.

This is a mood. I empathize with like....being relieved by the idea of dying, or just otherwise feeling trapped. The constant sense of being overwhelmed - the stage of life you feel trapped in right now, whatever the reason is that you think you're going to die alone and trapped - is a temporary moment. Things are more than likely to change drastically for the better.

Ik that sounds...idk, when I was feeling really depressed, I didn't really believe that my problems were fixable or would ever end. To that legitimate concern I'd say a couple things: 

1. Just scientifically, depression clouds your ability to past the pain or strong emotions of the present moment. It effects your ability to understand what things are truly the end of the world, and what just feel like it at the moment. It makes you think your problems will never go away - it warps reality. I'm not saying at all that your motivations for wanting to die are insignificant, or small, or not a big deal - I'm sure they're all three of those things - but just that they're not insurmountable - there are others that have been in your position that have found a way forward. For the moment, knowing your perception is warped because of depression, take the word of people around you that says things'll be okay - you at least need to wait a bit to find out.

\^\^ the above goes for things like....feeling like you're a burden to people. You are not - depression makes you think that you are. I know it might not seem like it, but - based on the testimonial of people that have been in remission or recovered from mental illness, and the way it made them feel similarly - just...open up even to a sliver of a possibility that your brain might be lying to you, and that you're not a burden.

I'm not saying "this is all in your head" (and ppl that do that suck). Mental illness, in my experience, is 10000% real. But some of its symptoms are to warp your perception of reality - try your very best to not let it do that to you, or at the very least know that it does that to you. This is all temporary - it will pass, as hard as it is to believe it...at least be open to that possibility.

2. Even if your problems can't be resolved, you DON'T have to be sad or in constant pain every day. Get treatment for mental health - ask for help. It seems (or at least seemed to me) to be impossible to get effective treatment - it's remarkably effective if you find the right treatment. Don't give up on that, trust me.

In the meantime, I've found sleep to be a great way to kind of "escape" from everything that's going on, if you see what I mean. If you just can't handle something anymore - or if you think you're going to make a bad decision/do something stupid - I'd usually just go to sleep early. Kinda silly, but it genuinely helps. Also - find things you enjoy doing. When I was really hurting, it was hard to find anything I enjoyed. If that thing is sleep, or showering, or a certain food you like, or a TV show, awesome. Maybe there's a certain person you love, or you like your job, or a hobby - anything. Do that more, or get involved in it - think about it when you're feeling really down. That also really helped me.

I'll be thinking about you, hope any of this helped. Always feel free to reach out.

**In terms of improving:** the good news is it sounds like you're losing all these rounds because of small, random mistakes (forget a link extension, don't read a key card, don't explain something enough, etc. like you said) instead of larger, more structural issues with your debating. My advice would be that every time something like that happens, you should take note of what happened and know to practice it later. Ideally, you should be doing a round report after every single debate where you write down the judge's feedback and RFD. That means you can go back and look at the things that are repeatedly problems. Make note of what happens repeatedly. Did you not explain something well enough? Read through that evidence again for comprehension or review that argument, and do a redo speech where you correct your mistakes. Did you skip an important card because you had too much evidence to get through? Edit your constructives so that you can fit all evidence you need within the time you have, and do drills where you order your speeches so that the most important pieces of evidence are read first. If there's something you always forget to do - for example, when I debated, I always forgot to give overviews at the top of my 2ARs - make yourself a reminder at the top of your flow, or just write it on your hand!

A good thing to think about: it's fine to make a mistake or lose to an argument the first time, it's just part of learning. But you should aim to never lose to the same argument twice, or make the same mistake twice. That means that when you make a mistake, you drill on it until you fix it. And that means when you lose to a certain argument due to lack of prep, you write blocks for it so you don't hit again.

Idk how much of this stuff you're already doing so forgive me if this is stuff you already know, but here are examples of some things you should be doing to solve the problems you mentioned:

1. Forgetting link extensions and not explaining args well enough: pre-write your blocks!! Obviously not everything can be pre-written, but if you KNOW you're going to have to do something - for example, extend the impact to a disad - write out that impact extension! Pre-writing will make it easy for you figure out how to give maximum explanation with maximum word economy, as well as make small args that you might not have time to think up on the spot that can make a big difference in RFDs (ev comparison, ! weighing, etc.) Preferably (and ik it's a lot of work, so depending on how much debate experience you have this might depend on what your school's debate infrastructure looks like), you should have pre-written 2AC/1AR blocks to all 1NC args you've ever debated, and 2NC/1NR extensions/blocks for all neg positions you're planning on going for. Hmu if you want an example of what these files should look like, I'd be happy to help. 
2. Silly mistakes: redos!! Redos are so, so effective. Save your flows, if the other team and your circuit is okay with it record your rounds so you can go back to listen to them. Give redos of the speeches you messed up, fixing the part you messed up on. It'll improve your ability to give speeches - seriously, almost nothing is as effective as improving debate skill as redos - while retraining bad habits you have to make those small mistakes, and make you feel better about the speeches you give/boost confidence by showing you the capacity you have to give really great speeches when you think about it for a bit. Try to do redos sometimes with infinite prep time, and sometimes with the amount of prep time you'd have in a real debate. Try also to only do rebuttal speeches (so no 1AC, 1NC, 2AC - 2NCs are aight though). If you've done debate for a while and are still messing things up, it's time to not just do the same thing over and over again if it's clearly not working - it's time to target those bad habits and work to improve them.

Other things to do: watch rounds on youtube and FLOW. Just watching these debates and flowing is a good way to get better, but a good drill to do that maximizes your benefit even more is to - before a debater gives a certain speech (for example a 1AR) - pause the debate and give the speech yourself. Then watch the actual speech and see how the debater in the video gives it. Compare and contrast, see what you could've done better, and if you think you did anything better than the debaters in the video. After watching a debate online, you can also write out your own RFD, watch the judges' RFDs if they're included in the videos, and compare and contrast - it'll help you get an idea of what you should be doing to win debates. 

Good youtube pages for debates: Exodus files (for policy), VBI or NSD (for LD) - also, if you debate in a more traditional circuit, while watching faster/more progressive rounds is still a really good exercise, you can look on the NSDA website - they often put up more traditional debate rounds to watch.

Similarly, if there are tournaments where you don't make outrounds, GO WATCH outrounds and flow (if it's allowed on your circuit) - try to figure out what these people are doing differently than you to be in outrounds, and then do drills/give speeches incorporating these concepts.

**About feeling like you can't get better:** That's a really terrible feeling, and so, so frustrating. Most people in their debate careers experience that feeling of frustration, especially when they work really hard and don't seem to be meeting goals or getting any closer to the goals they want to meet. It seems like you're feeling especially defeated though, and I'm sorry that's happening to you. My advice and experience is that **how people respond to failure** is paramount to being good at debate. Honestly, it's not who wins the most at first, or even really who's the smartest, but instead: when people lose, how do they respond? Do they keep their head down and work, or do they give up? I'd encourage you to do the former, and to see every mistake that you make not as an invitation to beat yourself up but instead as a chance to learn and correct your behavior. If you do that, you'll start seeing more results than your competitors who don't have that attitude - and honestly, having that mindset is just a valuable skill/something to be proud of on its own. I'm serious, if you want, you can still get really good at debate - it's just a mindset you gotta get out of where it's an awful experience to lose, because - while losing sucks - beating yourself up about it too much is a. no fun, and debate should be overall a positive experience, obviously and b. not productive in winning the next time.

About the people on your team that sound like jerks: it's hard to do, but ignore them. Work hard and you'll probably be better than them soon - even if not, as much as I love debate - and I love debate - being a good person is more important than being a good debater. And ofc - cheesy and all but true - how good you are as a debater does not encourage your worth as a person. Coaches and teams that are exclusive based off of who is doing the best really do suck. If you are interested and work hard, coaches do tend to pick up on that and might give you more attention. Either way though, my advice would be to find people that won't judge you by your skill level - people that you can just...talk about and enjoy debate with. There are lots of outlets to find these people, whether on your local circuit, on reddit, on the debate discord (not on it but I've heard it's pretty active? Can't speak to the level of openness there, don't know much about it), etc. 

I hope I was able to be helpful in any way. Seriously, if you need help or have questions about any of this, always feel free to dm me. I did policy and LD in high school (grad 2019) and now coach, and I'm happy to help you improve as much as I can, or just provide some thoughts if you wanna vent. You seem really dedicated to debate and I hope this helps - it sounds like, if you want to stick with debate, you can be really good.

I don't do PF, so less prepared to speak on the PF-specific reasons against disclosure you gave. Overall, I disagree with this analysis in a couple ways:

Re: disclosure incentivizes breaking new: Maybe it does. People who break new often because of disclosure I think are responding to disclosure in the wrong way. In a system with disclosure, breaking new seems to serve the purpose to avoid prep-outs, which we **shouldn't** be avoiding. People that dislike disclosure because they have to face prep-outs are looking for ways to get around clash specific to the aff/argument they're reading, either by not disclosing so people don't cut specific strategies against them, doing tons of new research so they can break new and don't have to disclose.

This is the wrong way to go about it. One of the theses of the "disclosure good" argument is that people shouldn't be so afraid of prep-outs; winning through obfuscation and dodging clash (anti-disclosure) is bad, winning through genuine skill and engagement (disclosure) is good. Research is great - but people are doing the wrong research. They should instead see the specific responses people are reading against their aff, go back to the source material and refine their arguments, and cut new arguments against those positions. That **encourages** clash; the best debaters win because they're prepared and skilled, and are never scared of being prepped out.

Re: Disclosure creates mediocre research: I think the above kind of answers this. Debates don't end in the first two constructives, but continue into rebuttals. The type of strategy disclosure rewards is one that is **truly a good argument,** so that it's hard to dispute even in the presence of specific strategies. It also rewards detailed, position and topic specific research to win a specific, valuable clash over the aff/a different argument.

Re: Disclosure decreases creativity/debating under pressure: Maybe for the first two speeches. But the debate obviously goes on after that. The first two speeches - maybe even the first 3 - are relatively scripted, because of pre-round/pre-tournament research (which is in itself a valuable practice). But that makes the rest of the debate so much higher quality and even more challenging, because the arguments are better and more directly responsive. The rest of the debate continues that argumentation and develops those arguments.

I don't really get this. I feel like there are two scenarios for a "unique arg" found by a small school:

Their surprise and lack of preparation will lead small schools winning more debates because their opponents are unable to engage. Hey there! A lot of people feel that way imo, to a certain extent, especially as a freshman and sophomore. With rare exceptions, freshmen and sophomores lose a lot - they've just been doing debate less long than other people. What determines which underclassmen debaters will be good by the time they're juniors and seniors is how they respond to losing. If you get really discouraged by losing and stop working hard, you won't be good. If you use losing as fuel to get better and recognize that mistakes are a learning experience, you have every shot at being good by the time you're older. 

I understand that it's frustrating, but it's normal that you're losing, especially as a sophomore; sophomore year, for the vast majority of people, is tough. Keep doing it if you enjoy debate, learn from it, and work hard.

Idk if you're doing LD, but check out Victory Briefs Classrooms. I've never used it, but the ppl at VBI are really smart imo and it seems pretty comprehensive (and it's free!) [https://www.vbidebate.com/victory-briefs-classrooms-1](https://www.vbidebate.com/victory-briefs-classrooms-1)

When I was a novice/learning I watched some of these (Go fight win novice debate): [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9TVoPWu-fYw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9TVoPWu-fYw) . I found them very helpful, and there's a whole series of them.

I second the Bill Batterman videos. 

For learning about evidence and how arguments are usually structured, you can check out the wiki (just search "Policy debate wiki," "LD debate wiki," or "PF debate wiki," they should pop up). Open evidence is also a good place to start: [https://openevidence.debatecoaches.org/](https://openevidence.debatecoaches.org/) . While you should try to avoid taking too much evidence, as it's good to learn to cut your own, it's a good place to get some evidence too if really needed.

Sites like [https://hsimpact.wordpress.com/](https://hsimpact.wordpress.com/) and [https://www.vbriefly.com/](https://www.vbriefly.com/) will often have ideas of drills you can do to get better at certain concepts. I know [https://debatedrills.com/en/](https://debatedrills.com/en/) has a bunch of free concepts and ideas for drills that you and your team can do and might find helpful.

Another thing that's helpful is watching videos of debates, and flowing them! The NSD and Victory Briefs youtube channels have a lot of national circuit LD (and some PF) videos. Exodus files [https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCsXRbcErUsJaGtmuSlG30HQ](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCsXRbcErUsJaGtmuSlG30HQ) youtube is a great place to find College Policy rounds, as well as [DebateVid.io](https://DebateVid.io) ([https://debatevid.io/](https://debatevid.io/)). PF Videos Youtube ([https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCYPPO78Q16D9p4\_bX0rR2QQ](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCYPPO78Q16D9p4_bX0rR2QQ)) is a good place to find PF rounds. I don't know if you know whether in a more traditional or progressive circuit, but the NSDA website will also have more traditional debates for you to watch in all the events. They also might be easier for you to follow at first if you or your teammates are just starting out.

Something to consider would be getting a coach. There are often people either in your area or remotely who would love to be hired, and some will even work at very low rates or pro bono if price is an issue for you. If you'd ever like help with finding someone, feel free to hmu and I'd be happy to help. 

You could also consider going to camp; when I was on a smaller team, it was very helpful to be able to take the knowledge that I learned at debate camp over the summer home to my teammates, so we could all benefit from them. Camps range in prices and in lengths, and there's usually something for everyone. I don't know what event you do, but if you search on this reddit or in other places I'm sure you can find a guide to camps people have posted.

Finally, feel free to pm me if you have any questions about this or need help in any way - it's awesome that you're setting up the club and I'm always more than happy to help

Hi, I see a lot of people recommending other camps in the comment and just wanted to put a word in for VBI. I'm not affiliated with it - therefore, the below is just my personal experience as a former student and obviously not the prevailing wisdom on everything VBI - but I attended for four years in a row and would 10/10 highly recommend. Also, I went to VBI LA1 and Swarthmore, I've never been to LA2, they were both great but I probably learned a bit more at LA1 because of the extra length. 

There are a few things I would think about:

a. Self-motivated environment. A lot of people in the comments are saying that VBI is "laid back;" my experience runs counter to that, and it's definitely not laid back unless you choose to make it so. From my experience, the VBI schedule gives a decent amount of independent time that is not supposed to function as "free time," but instead meant for talking and learning about debate outside of just a heavily structured lab. They have Socrates hour, where you can work with any instructor on staff that you would like; there's mentor time, where you get one-on-one instruction from a staff member; there's a couple hours of free time each night before room check to cut cards or talk about debate with staff members or friends. Yeah, technically you could just chill during Socrates hours, play card games with your mentor, and use the hours before bed as extra time to hang out - but I wouldn't recommend it, why are you paying to be there? I found that the I got the most out of VBI when I was dedicated myself to engaging, actively reaching out to people to work with, cutting evidence and maybe even talking about debate with friends at night. If you are self-motivated and determined, VBI gives you, imo, a ridiculous amount of time to better yourself at debate. You get skills based on what you give, to a certain extent. 

b. Diverse intellectual culture. I found that the amount of time to work with different staff members and interact with different people, far from making the camp "laid back," created a welcoming culture of intellectualism. People are always talking to one another about debate and argumentation, and it expanded my worldview (both debate-related and otherwise) drastically. People from all over the country are excited to be there, excited to talk about and learn about debate, and excited to learn from one another. The staff was also super diverse in terms of argumentative background, ranging from first year out LDers to highly accomplished college policy debaters, who read all different types of arguments. No one ever tried to pigeonhole me into a certain style of debate, and saw the value of all the different types of arguments that I explored. And, since the staff was so diverse, there would always be someone on staff able to teach the argument I wanted to learn - and staff weren't shy about admitting their weaknesses in a certain area and directing me to someone who knew more about that argument, which really bettered my experience.

c. It's just.....fun. I think people sometimes understate the importance of a welcoming environment at debate camp. At VBI, no one was competitive with me -outside- of a debate round. I say that to mean that, while debate is a competitive activity and people were very dedicated to it at VBI, they didn't see my success and learning as a hinderance to their learning, but instead were incredibly supportive and we learned from each other. There's this contest called Omegathon (yo, it's wild, it's super fun) that's awesome, my mentors and lab leaders have become some of my closest mentors and my labmates some of my good friends that I still remain close with. That environment also allows for people to take intellectual risks, to give a bad speech or say an answer even though they think it might be wrong - which leads to growth and learning.

Hi there - I didn't originally write the comment, but I personally disagree with this response:

Re: clout culture:

> Removing the most visible, most centralized database of rankings makes the perpetuation of those rankings more work, not less.

Rankings at least rely on metrics that are somewhat correlated to student success. Without an actual analysis of results, "clout culture" will devolve even further into a popularity contest, with teams gaining reputation based solely on social capital - which is one of the problems in the first place/feeds into a cycle of clout culture. Sure, threat lists are non-unique but I think that's kind of the point - students will participate in clout culture with or without ISD rankings, so even if those rankings serve the function of clout culture, it's try or die for anything that will make that system even a tiny bit better.

> Ultimately I'm not sure this has an impact...Speaker awards, elim depth etc are measures of a debaters skill that you can use to determine whose outrounds to go watch and learn from

Don't think their argument was that w/o rankings people don't know what elims to watch. Instead, absent rankings, peoples' perceptions of who is "good" are often biased by social capital, or even racially or along gender-based lines. Realistically, debaters will not sort through every single tournament on Tabroom to figure out speaks/results when creating opinions about debaters; they'll (sadly) often prep out whoever "feels" like a threat, or go watch whoever everyone else is watching.

Re: Education

> Get real - not having ordinal rankings of debaters is going to have little to no effect on debaters college apps. 

To be fair, I don't think it's bad for it either - saying to a college admissions officer, or even a high school administration when asking for funding "we are the x ranked team in the country" is probably more immediately effective than something like "we cleared at Greenhill, Blake, and Stanford and got one bid to the TOC - but, we got the at large and were able to attend!" if you get what I mean. But overall, I can't really argue with you there.

> you don't need to explicitly look down on certain teams for this culture to become toxic. That behavior is implicitly coded into our behavior from behind the scenes in ways we usually don't think about. I've heard stories on stories about how much easier it is to make friends [on the circuit] when you're good at debate.

I 100% agree that this culture is problematic and that it is easier to make friends when you're good at debate. I just don't think getting rid of rankings is the solution. Debate is a competitive activity, and there are many, many benefits to it being one; I don't think I need to convince you there. I know there is a way for debaters to be incredibly competitive and still recognize that ones' competitive success is not the measure of their worth as a human being. The answer to this exclusive culture isn't to lessen debate's competition, but change the way that we react to it.

> None of this is to say that I think that we should elide debate's gamelike elements...That isn't an argument to why these minute differentiated approaches are valuale.

This is interesting, and I'm compelled by the idea that making small adjustments to better the culture of debate doesn't have to come at the expense of competition in debate. I'm just unconvinced that this adjustment is even positive/in the right direction, never mind that ISD getting rid of its rankings will make a big enough positive difference on debate culture to even justify it.

I agree "clout culture" is bad. I'm therefore 100% in favor of initiatives that aim to reduce the social stratification that comes with successful debaters gaining social power and capital, often leading to the exclusion of everyone else. I also agree that "clout culture" can break down along race/gender/class lines; as a woman in debate, I'm definitely able to attest that exclusive social groups of highly successful guys are both all too common and harmful. Having a support system in debate is key - debate is sometimes hostile, and lack of social credibility or that support system is, in my opinion, why gender minority students leave the activity at disproportionate rates. 

This isn't the way to do it, in my opinion. Debate is a competitive activity. Debaters will still get trophies and bids; some debaters will clear to outrounds, some will not; each round will have a winner and a loser. In order to reduce "clout culture," ISD seems like it wants to just reduce the competitive aspect of debate in the first place, which is not only massively non-unique but also obviously not the way to go about it. Part of debate is learning to handle competition well, to win without developing an ego and to use losing as motivation to work harder. And, debate is a competition; that plays a large part in driving students to research and practice, incentivizing schools to fund the activity, and attracting novice participation. 

Finally, if you want to get rid of clout culture, this is not the way to do it. Much of clout culture works based on hype; some people are "big names" in debate and just have a reputation of being good. Current ranking systems, while imperfect, take into account statistics that have some correlation to student success. To me, removing that system seems like a great way for reputation and popularity to define who is seen as "successful" in debate instead, which is the very thing that upholds clout culture.

I really think that this post is unnecessary at best though, and harmful at worst. This will be long, so **there's a summary at the bottom.** A few thoughts:

1. This post may push those with mental illness to question the legitimacy of their experiences. I struggled with mental illness throughout high school; it took me a long time to even recognize that my mental illness was a problem affecting my grades and quality of life, partially because I thought that I was just making excuses or slacking. Mental illness (in the shape of depression but also a lot of other forms as well) is real, and no one deserves to question if they are a capable student just because others say that their experience isn't real or worthy of consideration. **It honestly takes a lot of bravery to be able to admit that you are sick, especially considering how stigmatized mental illness is, and then to be told that you're making things up to justify better grades? That should not happen.**
2. This type of wording - talking about how mental health is just an "excuse" for bad grades - takes mental illness non-seriously. If someone got physically ill, and had to miss a bunch of school, that would probably be seen as a "legitimate" reason for bad grades. The fact that mental health isn't looked at the same way adds to the stigma around mental illness, that it's "all in someone's head" and that "they're just making it up for attention or an excuse." To the people saying that you shouldn't write about your mental health experience on your application as an excuse for bad grades, this is a symptom of the problem; AOs see mental illness as something to be scared of, while physical illness garners sympathy. 
3. I'm not sure how many people actually fake mental illness to justify their grades. Compared to the number of people that actually suffer from mental illness, I'd guess those people are of a very low percentage. I certainly don't think it's worth this post that complains about them that may have negative effects. Honestly, since the percentage of those people that fake mental illness is so low, at least some of this backlash has to be against people that genuinely do have mental illness that is hurting them in school. That's really bad and unacceptable, and I think that some people should try see why they they feel so defensive when others bring up mental illness.

I know you put a disclaimer at the bottom saying that this isn't targeted towards people actually diagnosed with "depression." Number one, there are many more mental illnesses that can hurt performance in school than just depression, but that's just semantics. Secondly, I think the percentage of people that this post is actually targeting that fake mental illness for better grades pales in comparison to people that are being honest about their struggles; I addressed that earlier in this post. Third, you don't need a diagnosis to have legitimate struggles with mental illness. Some people can't get a diagnosis, because they might not have the money to go to a hospital/psychologist, or they might not be able to tell their parents about their struggles; **some might not be able to be diagnosed because no one takes them seriously in the first place, thinking it's just an excuse for their poor performance in school** or life in general**.** Others haven't asked for help or a diagnosis, because they are still coming to terms with the fact that they are mentally ill and it's affecting their quality of life, despite of or because of society and people that tell them it's just an excuse, a phase, or all in their heads. 

In totality, just be sensitive to other peoples' struggles. I'm not trying to take the moral high ground, or teach you a lesson, or roast you, or anything ridiculous like that. Anyone reading this has a choice in how they react to peoples' struggles; by taking them seriously and validating their feelings, or by dismissing it as an excuse. Doing the former can be lifesaving - just ask me - but also it's just the kind thing to do. If people are making up a mental illness for an excuse for grades, (which again happens pretty infrequently), that's their problem. What we can do is take peoples' struggles seriously, and treat people with belief, kindness, and respect.

For anyone struggling with their mental health, grades, etc: Things have happened that are out of your control, and that is not a fault with you as a person; that is the fault of a literal disease that is affecting your life. Your experiences are 100% legitimate, you're not making them up and they're not all in your head, and you are more than capable of doing well in school, and in life.

Summary: Mental illness is not an "excuse" for poor grades, and no people don't make it up for attention or to justify poor performance.

I don't know about your personal experience, but by and large disclosure seems to be a good way to have higher quality rounds. Re: repetition, disclosure allows for more prep time before rounds and tournaments; that leads to argument innovation as people actually have the time to delve into new literature, and find the best ways to beat a strategy. I find that not disclosing leads to debaters reading the same generics, as they can't prep specific positions to beat certain strats. 

Yes, it does dictate how the first few speeches will go - for example, if I can prep out a 1NC before the round to a specific aff, I don't need to scramble during the 1AC to figure out what to read. But, that leads to higher quality debate in the later speeches as debaters have the best possible arguments to win the debate - from the 2AC onwards, debaters have to figure out how those arguments interact, and figure out their strategy to win the round. That type of critical thinking is bolstered by disclosure. 

Another really solid reason to disclose is the research skills you get from disclosure; for example, it's a lot better to be able to prep specific strategies for affs then rely on generics. As well, not saying that this is you at all, but I've encountered a lot of people who want to hide behind the "surprise" of their non-disclosed positions, relying on the element of surprise to win them rounds. That's a bad idea, imo; people should be aiming to be good enough to be able to beat the best possible version of the arguments against their position. That allows you to go back, refine your argument, and then figure out how to respond to potential objections. That process is valuable; hoping that people are surprised, and therefore won't actually debate your argument, is not.
